explanations.explanation: Close, friend, but David leaves his own strength out of it. He says, "In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him." The word is "alone," so there's no room for a second helper on that line. Even a stamper with a mustache this big can't rest on his own muscle.

That's right, friend. David says, "In God alone my soul finds rest…" There's no "and my own strength" tacked on the end. His rest comes from God, and so does his salvation. I tried resting on my own strength once, and I'm telling you, my mustache gave out before I did.

That's it, baker. David says, "He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken." Rock and fortress are about as sturdy as it gets. David's standing there like a pan that never warps, and I'm proud of him.
Nice thought, friend, but that's not what David says here. He says, "I will never be shaken." Being alone never comes up in the verse. It's about staying steady, with God as his rock and fortress.

explanations.answer: He will never lose a battle
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, with a fortress in the picture. But David doesn't say a word about battles in this verse. He says, "I will never be shaken." That's his confidence, and it rests on who God is, not on a win-loss record.

explanations.answer: Cast him down from his lofty perch
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says, "They fully intend to cast him down from his lofty perch…" Fully intend! They didn't wander into it, they came with a whole plan. And still David tells his soul to rest in God (Psalm 62:5).

explanations.answer: Drive him out of the land
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. It says they "…fully intend to cast him down from his lofty perch…" Nothing about chasing him out of the land. Their aim is to bring him down from the high spot he's on.

Not this time, baker. The verse says they "…fully intend to cast him down from his lofty perch…" Riches don't show up in it. Later in the psalm David does talk about riches, but he's warning people there not to set their hearts on them (Psalm 62:10).

That's the one, baker. "with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse." Smiling on the outside, cursing on the inside. That's like a cookie box with a pretty bow and nothing but crumbs rattling around in there.
Ooh, friend, that's a sneaky one, but the verse says something heavier. "with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse." The blessing is only on the outside. Inside, it's cursing.

I like the drama, baker, but nobody's crying in this verse. David says, "with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse." The nice words are covering what's really inside. Tears aren't part of it.

You got it, baker. David says, "Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him." His hope has one source, and he's talking to his own soul about it. I do that too, mostly when the dough won't cooperate.

Good try, friend, but the verse says nothing about quiet enemies. David's reason is this: "…for my hope comes from Him." His rest rests on God, not on a calm day. In fact, he's just been describing people who bless with their mouths and curse inside (Psalm 62:4).

That would be a nice reason, baker, but David doesn't give it. He says, "Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him." The reason is where his hope comes from. Nobody's holding up a scoreboard.

True, baker! David says, "Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him." He's been talking to his own soul, and now he turns to everyone else. Pouring out your heart before God means holding nothing back, and I think that sounds like a relief.

Not quite, friend. It's true. David says, "Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him." He turns from his own soul to the people, and that's the invitation. Then he adds, "God is our refuge."

That's it, baker. David says, "Weighed on the scale, they go up; together they are but a vapor." When the scale goes up, there's hardly anything on it. Picture a scale with a puff of steam on it, and it just bobs there like it's embarrassed.
Whoa, friend, flip that one over. David says they "go up" on the scale, and that they are "…but a vapor…" A scale that goes up has almost nothing on it. Gold would pull it down hard.

explanations.answer: They weigh more than they look
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but it's the other direction, baker. David says, "Weighed on the scale, they go up; together they are but a vapor." Going up means light, not heavy. Vapor isn't hiding any secret weight.

Careful, friend, that one's flipped. David says, "If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them." He doesn't say riches are the problem. He says don't give them your heart. A heart that big belongs somewhere sturdier.

Right, baker. David says, "If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them." Just before that he says, "Place no trust in extortion or false hope in stolen goods." Money can come in, but your heart shouldn't move in with it.
You got it, baker. David says, "God has spoken once; I have heard this twice: that power belongs to God…" Whatever else is loud in the world, the power is God's. That's the line to hold onto.
Nice try, friend, but David doesn't say that. What he heard twice is "that power belongs to God…" It's about whose power it is, not about what his enemies will do. Nobody's running in this verse.

I understand the guess, since David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), baker. But the verse says he heard "that power belongs to God…" Nothing about his kingdom lasting. The power is God's, and that's the whole point.
That's right, baker. David says, "For You will repay each man according to his deeds." Not by bank account, not by family name. It's what a person has done. That's how David closes the psalm.
Close to the theme, friend, but not the word. David just said not to set your heart on riches. He ends with, "…You will repay each man according to his deeds." Wealth isn't the measuring stick.

Good guess, since David mentioned the lowborn, baker. But the verse says, "…You will repay each man according to his deeds." Whether a person is lowborn or exalted isn't what he names here. Deeds are the word.
